summary: Umar recounts how, angered to hear that his sister had accepted Islaam, he struck her and then took the manuscript she was reading.
notes: Ends with 'The rest of the narration continues.' The sister and her husband are named only in the heading, so they are not tagged.

summary: Uthmaan bin Madh'oon gives up Waleed bin Mughiera's protection, then is slapped in the eye for disputing a poet's couplets with the Quraysh.

people.name: Labeed bin Rabee'ah bin Maalik bin Kilaab Qaysi

notes: Ends at the heading of Ali's couplets, which are not included. Labeed is the poet who later embraced Islaam, so he is tagged as a Companion.

summary: A poem lamenting those who struck Uthmaan bin Madh'oon and warning that Allaah will punish them.
notes: The poet is not named in this text. The preceding narration attributes the couplets to Ali.

summary: Waleed asks Uthmaan bin Madh'oon to return under his protection, and Uthmaan refuses.
notes: Ibn Is'haaq is cited only as the source and is not tagged.

summary: Mus'ab bin Umayr, once Makkah's most pampered youth, accepts Islaam in secret, is jailed by his family, and endures hardship after returning from Abyssinia.
notes: The opening narrator line is garbled ('Hadhrat Muhammad ﷺ narrated from his; father'). The narrator is not tagged. Uthmaan bin Talha is tagged as a Companion; he is not the approved 'talha' (Talha bin Ubaydillaah).

summary: Abdullaah bin Hudhaafa refuses to leave Islaam under torture by the Roman emperor, and Umar kisses his head after he is freed.
notes: Abu Raafi may be the approved 'raafi' (Raafi, unsure); not matched because the list gives only 'Raafi'.

summary: Ibn Abbaas tells Sa'eed bin Jubayr how severely the Mushrikeen tortured Muslims, to the point that some said words of disbelief to save their lives.
After the Hijrah to Madinah the Muslims faced attacks from the Arabs, and Allaah revealed Surah Noor verse 55 promising them succession and peace.
A second report from Ubay bin Ka'b gives the same occasion for Surah Noor verse 55: the Arab attacks on the Muslims after the Hijrah.
notes: Variant of n00328.

summary: Abu Moosa Ash'ari recounts the scarcity on the Dhaatur Riqaa expedition, when his feet were cut and his nails fell off, and the expedition was named after the bandages.
Abu Burda relays that Abu Moosa disliked telling the Dhaatur Riqaa story because it made his good deeds known, and said Allaah would reward it.
notes: The bracketed comment at the end is the translator's, not part of the narration.

summary: Nu'maan bin Basheer and Umar describe how the Prophet often could not find even poor dates to fill his stomach.
notes: Two reports: Nu'maan bin Basheer, then Umar's statement during his Khilaafah.

summary: Abu Hurayra finds the Prophet praying seated from hunger, and the Prophet tells him that a hungry person who endures it for reward will not face strict reckoning on the Day of Qiyaamah.
Aa'isha recounts the family of Abu Bakr sending a goat's leg, which she and the Prophet cut up without a lantern.
Asked whether the meat was cut by lantern light, Aa'isha says they had no oil for a lantern and would have eaten the oil rather than burn it.
notes: The questioner is unnamed.

summary: Abu Hurayra says the Prophet's wives went months without a lantern or fire, rubbing any oil on their bodies rather than burning it.
Abu Hurayra says two months passed without a fire in the Prophet's house, and they lived on dates and water, with milk sent by Ansaar neighbours.
Urwa relays Aa'isha's account of two months without a fire in the Prophet's rooms, living on dates and water, with the milk from Ansaar neighbours that the Prophet gave them to drink.
Aa'isha says the Prophet's house sometimes went forty days without fire, living on dates and water when they could find them.
Aa'isha weeps when she eats her fill, remembering that the Prophet never ate bread or meat to his fill twice in one day.
Aa'isha says the Prophet never ate barley bread to his fill for three days, or wheat bread for two days, and at his death he could not fill himself even with dates and water.
notes: Three reports, all from Aa'isha.

summary: Aa'isha says the Prophet never filled himself for three days in a row, though they could have, because he preferred to give to others.
notes: Bayhaqi is cited only as the source and is not tagged.

summary: Hasan and Anas describe the Prophet patching his own clothes, going three days without both lunch and dinner, and never eating from a table or fine bread.
notes: Two reports (Hasan, then Anas) and 'another narration'. The text gives only the name Hasan, which may not be the Companion.

summary: Ibn Abbaas narrates that the Prophet's family often went hungry at night, and that their most common bread was made of barley.
Abu Hurayra refuses an invitation to a roasted goat, saying the Prophet left the world without eating his fill of even barley bread.
Anas narrates that Faatima gave the Prophet a piece of barley bread, which he said was the first food he had eaten in three days.
notes: Tabraani is cited only as a source and is not tagged.

summary: Abu Hurayra reports that when hot food was brought to the Prophet, he praised Allaah, saying he had not eaten hot food for a long time.
Sahl bin Sa'd says that from the start of the Prophet's mission until his death the Prophet never saw fine white flour or a sift, so they ate barley that had been blown clean rather than sifted.
Aa'isha says no barley bread was ever left on the Prophet's tablecloth, and another narration says no food was left when it was lifted.
notes: Two narrations from Aa'isha.

summary: Abu Talha says the Companions showed the Prophet their stomachs with stones tied to them from hunger, and the Prophet showed his own two stones; Ibn Bujayr adds the Prophet's warning about the Day of Qiyaamah.
notes: Two reports: Abu Talha, then Ibn Bujayr with a warning about the Hereafter.

summary: Aa'isha says overeating is the first calamity to hit this Ummah after the Prophet's death, weakening hearts and strengthening carnal desires.
notes: Only one approved theme fits; the main topic is moderation in eating.

summary: Ibn Abbaas narrates how the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar, all hungry, were fed by Abu Ayyoob, and how the Prophet later gave Abu Ayyoob a slave woman, whom he freed.
Umar tells how the Prophet met him and Abu Bakr, both hungry, and took them to the house of the Ansaari Abul Haytham bin Tayyihaan.
notes: Ends with 'A lengthy Hadith follows'; the rest is not included. Abul Haytham may be the approved 'abul-haysim' (listed as Anas bin Raafi, unsure), but the names differ, so he is not matched.

summary: Faatima recounts that the family had no food, and the Prophet found her sons out with Ali; Ali relates finding a lost dinar that bought bread, and that he later paid far more zakaah.
notes: Three reports: Faatima's account, Ataa's report of Ali's dinar, and Muhammad bin Ka'b's report of Ali's zakaah. Hasan and Husayn are the Prophet's grandsons; the text names them only as Hasan and Husayn.

summary: Ummu Sulaym relates that the Prophet told her to be patient, since his household had gone seven days without food and three days without fire, though he could ask Allaah to turn the mountains of Tihaama into gold.
Sa'd recounts that he and the Prophet in Makkah endured hard times patiently, and that he survived three days by drinking water after grinding and toasting a piece of camel leather.
Sa'd describes how, in battles with the Prophet, the Companions had only acacia and lotus leaves to eat, and he was the first Arab to shoot an arrow in Allaah's path.
notes: Cut off mid-sentence after 'because it was not at all'; the rest is missing.

summary: Miqdaad relates that, starving, he drank the Prophet's share of milk, and after the Prophet prayed for them he found the goats full again and milked them for the Prophet.
notes: Two reports: the main account, then 'another narration' of his arrival in Madinah in groups of ten with the Ansaar. The text spells him Miqdaad bin Aswad; the list has Miqdaad bin Amr, who is the same man.

summary: Mujaahid relays how Abu Hurayra, starving, was invited home by the Prophet, who sent him to call the people of Suffa, served them milk, and told him to drink what remained.
notes: The footnote 'Abu Nu'aym in Hilya' is inserted into the text and is not part of the narration. Abu Bakr and Umar passed by without inviting him.

summary: Abu Hurayra says he went three days without eating, and the Prophet fed him from the leftovers shared with the people of Suffa until he was full.
